title: Your Cat's Tongue Has 300 Tiny Hooks 🐱
description:
Why is a cat's tongue so rough? It's covered in about 300 tiny backward-facing hooks called papillae, made of keratin, and each tip is a hollow scoop that wicks saliva down through the fur to the skin, cleaning out tangles and cooling the cat as it dries.

Sources:
https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/cat-tongues-keep-them-cool
https://www.sci.news/biology/cat-tongues-06638.html

Animated in the Chalkboard Lesson style.

topic: Why is a cat's tongue so rough?
script:
Why does your cat's tongue feel like sandpaper?
It's covered in about 300 tiny hooks,
all pointing backwards.
Each hook is a spine called a papilla,
made of keratin,
the same stuff as your fingernails.
But the weirdest part?
The tip of every spine is hollow,
a tiny scoop, like a quill pen.
When a cat licks,
those scoops sip up saliva,
slide down through the fur,
and drop it onto the skin.
That pulls out dirt and tangles,
and as the spit dries,
it cools the cat down.
Scientists think grooming handles
up to a quarter of a cat's cooling.
No wonder cats spend up to a quarter
of their waking hours licking themselves.
Researchers built a hairbrush
copying the cat's tongue.
So would you brush your hair
with three hundred tiny hooks?
key_facts: A cat's tongue has hundreds of backward-facing spines (filiform papillae); about 300 contact the fur with each lick (Noel & Hu, PNAS 2018)
The papillae are made of keratin, the same protein as fingernails
Each papilla tip has a hollow U-shaped scoop, like a quill-pen nib, that wicks saliva by surface tension
The papillae reach down through the fur to the skin, delivering saliva there and removing debris and tangles
Grooming evaporation may account for up to a quarter of a cat's cooling; domestic cats spend up to a quarter of their waking hours grooming
Researchers made a cat-tongue-inspired hairbrush that is easier to clean
